topics.name: Lead (element)
topics.kicker: Element 82 · The soft, heavy metal of old pipes, paint, and batteries
topics.briefing: Lead is a soft, heavy, bluish-gray metal that people have used for thousands of years; the Romans made water pipes from it, and its Latin name, plumbum, gave us the word “plumbing.” Car batteries and the heavy aprons worn during X-rays still use it. Because lead is poisonous, especially to children, it was taken out of gasoline and house paint, and the “lead” in your pencil is really harmless graphite.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: The inert pair effect explains why this element’s +2 oxidation state is far more stable than its +4 state, unlike the lighter members of its group. This element’s most common isotope has a “doubly magic” nucleus, because both its number of protons and its number of neutrons are magic numbers.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this soft, heavy metal with atomic number 82, whose symbol comes from the Latin word plumbum.

tossups.p: Clair Patterson measured isotopes of this element in meteorites to calculate in 1956 that Earth is about 4.55 billion years old. During that work, Patterson discovered how much of this element people had spread into the environment, and he spent years campaigning to get it out of gasoline.
tossups.r: Uranium slowly decays into this element. For 10 points, name this toxic metal with atomic number 82.

tossups.p: Working for General Motors in 1921, Thomas Midgley Jr. found that a compound of this metal with four ethyl groups stopped car engines from “knocking.” The United States banned gasoline containing that compound for cars in 1996, because this metal is toxic.
tossups.r: This metal was also taken out of house paint. For 10 points, name this heavy metal with atomic number 82.

tossups.p: Gaston Planté [“plahn-TAY”] invented the first rechargeable battery in 1859 using sheets of this metal in sulfuric acid. In a car battery, plates of this metal and of its dioxide both turn into this metal’s sulfate as the battery runs down.
tossups.r: Its main ore is the mineral galena. For 10 points, name this dense metal with atomic number 82.

tossups.p: In 1746, John Roebuck began making sulfuric acid on a large scale inside huge chambers lined with sheets of this metal, which resists attack by that acid. Ancient Romans bent sheets of this soft metal into water pipes.
tossups.r: The word “plumbing” comes from this metal’s Latin name. For 10 points, name this heavy element with atomic number 82.

tossups.p: Alchemists linked this metal with the planet Saturn, so poisoning by it was once called “saturnism.” For centuries, artists painted with a white pigment made from a carbonate of this metal, until safer titanium and zinc whites mostly replaced it.
tossups.r: This metal was banned from U.S. house paint in 1978. For 10 points, name this element with atomic number 82.

tossups.p: Below about 7 kelvins, this metal becomes a superconductor that carries electric current with no resistance. Because it melts at only about 327 degrees Celsius, this soft, dense metal is easy to cast into fishing sinkers and the heavy weights in sailboat keels.
tossups.r: Aprons containing this metal protect patients during X-rays. For 10 points, name this element with atomic number 82.

tossups.p: Ancient Athens paid for its warships with silver from the mines at Laurium, where the silver was separated from ores of this metal. Early “crystal radio” sets used a thin wire touching a cube-shaped crystal of galena, a sulfide of this metal.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this toxic metal, whose chemical symbol comes from the Latin word plumbum.

tossups.p: After Flint, Michigan, switched its water source in 2014 without treating the water to control corrosion, this metal began dissolving from old pipes into people’s tap water. Health agencies say there is no known safe level of this metal in a child’s blood.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this toxic heavy metal, which was also removed from gasoline and house paint.

tossups.p: The uranium-238 decay series ends with this element’s stable isotope of mass number 206, and the thorium-232 series ends with its isotope of mass number 208. Geologists measure uranium and this element in tiny zircon crystals to find the ages of ancient rocks.
tossups.r: This metal is used in car batteries. For 10 points, name this heavy metal with atomic number 82.

tossups.p: Flerovium, element 114, sits directly below this element on the periodic table. Traditional solder for joining wires and pipes is an alloy of tin and this element, which sits just below tin in the carbon group.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this soft, toxic metal that ancient Romans used to make water pipes.

tossups.p: The word “miniature” comes from minium, a bright red oxide of this metal that medieval artists used to decorate handwritten books. That same red oxide was later painted onto iron and steel to keep them from rusting.
tossups.r: Its main ore is galena. For 10 points, name this heavy metal with atomic number 82.

tossups.p: In the 1670s, George Ravenscroft developed a sparkling English glass that gets its brilliance from an oxide of this metal. Thick windows made of that same kind of glass let scientists safely watch radioactive materials.
tossups.r: Aprons containing this metal protect patients from X-rays. For 10 points, name this dense, poisonous element with atomic number 82.

tossups.p: Graphite was once called plumbago because people mistook it for an ore of this metal. That old mistake is why the gray core of a pencil is still named after this metal, even though pencils contain none of it.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this toxic heavy metal, whose chemical symbol comes from the Latin word plumbum.

tossups.p: Mixing solutions of potassium iodide and a nitrate of this metal makes a bright yellow solid. When that solid dissolves in hot water and then cools, it forms glittering flakes nicknamed “golden rain.”
tossups.r: This metal sits just below tin in group 14. For 10 points, name this element with atomic number 82.

clues.t: Element with atomic number 82; its symbol comes from the Latin word plumbum
Romans made water pipes from it, so the word “plumbing” comes from its Latin name
A toxic heavy metal that harms the brain and nervous system, especially in young children
In the U.S., it was banned from house paint in 1978 and from gasoline for cars in 1996
The gray core of a pencil is named after it, but it is really graphite, a form of carbon
Car batteries use plates of it and its dioxide soaked in sulfuric acid
So dense that it blocks radiation; aprons containing it protect patients during X-rays
Its main ore is galena, a shiny, cube-shaped sulfide mineral
In group 14, the carbon group, just below tin; flerovium (element 114) sits below it
Traditional solder is an alloy of tin and this metal, and old pewter often contained it
Soft enough to scratch with a fingernail, very dense, and melts at only about 327 °C
The stable end product of the uranium and thorium radioactive decay series
In 1921, Thomas Midgley Jr. found that a compound of it with four ethyl groups stopped engine “knocking” in gasoline
In 2014, Flint, Michigan, switched water sources, and it dissolved from old pipes into tap water
The inert pair effect makes its +2 oxidation state more stable than its +4 state
Its most common isotope, mass number 208, has a “doubly magic” nucleus; it is the heaviest element with stable isotopes
Clair Patterson used its isotopes in meteorites to date Earth at about 4.55 billion years (1956), then fought to get it out of gasoline
Geologists date ancient rocks by measuring uranium and this metal in zircon crystals
Gaston Planté invented the first rechargeable battery, using sheets of it, in 1859
John Roebuck’s 1746 process made sulfuric acid in huge chambers lined with it
Alchemists linked it with the planet Saturn, so poisoning by it was called “saturnism”
For centuries, artists painted with a white pigment made from its carbonate
Minium, its bright red oxide, decorated medieval books (giving us “miniature”) and kept iron from rusting
George Ravenscroft’s sparkling 1670s glass, known as crystal, gets its brilliance from its oxide
Graphite was once called plumbago because people mistook it for an ore of this metal
It becomes a superconductor below about 7 kelvins
Its iodide is a bright yellow solid that recrystallizes from hot water into glittering “golden rain” flakes
Galena crystals were detectors in early crystal radios; the silver from Athens’s Laurium mines came from its ores

trap.title: Not graphite, not tin
trap.body: Pencil cores carry this element’s name, but they are really graphite, a form of carbon, so a tossup about pencils or plumbago may want graphite or carbon instead. Tin is the other trap: it sits just above this element in group 14, and the two metals were mixed together in solder and pewter. Mercury, another toxic heavy metal, also tempts early buzzers.
trap.fix: Atomic number 82, plumbum, galena, car batteries, X-ray aprons, and old gasoline and paint point here. Tin is element 50 (its symbol, Sn, comes from stannum) and coats “tin cans”; mercury is the liquid metal in old thermometers.

topics.name: Fluorine
topics.kicker: Element 9 · The most reactive and most electronegative element
topics.briefing: Fluorine is the wildest element on the periodic table: this pale yellow gas reacts with almost everything, and it pulls on electrons harder than any other atom. It was so dangerous to isolate that chemists tried for decades before Henri Moissan finally succeeded in 1886. Tamed in compounds, it is everywhere: fluoride in toothpaste fights cavities, and nonstick Teflon pans are coated with a plastic made of carbon and fluorine.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Several chemists were poisoned or injured in failed attempts to isolate this element before Henri Moissan [“mwah-SAHN”] finally succeeded in 1886, using electrolysis in a chilled platinum apparatus. Moissan won the 1906 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for that work.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this pale yellow gas, the lightest halogen and the most electronegative element.

tossups.p: In an 1812 letter to Humphry Davy, André-Marie Ampère [“ahm-PAIR”] suggested a name for this element, decades before anyone managed to isolate it. A mineral made of calcium and this element defines a hardness of 4 on the Mohs scale.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this element with atomic number 9, whose ion, fluoride, is added to toothpaste.

tossups.p: While working on refrigerant gases at DuPont in 1938, Roy Plunkett accidentally discovered a slippery plastic made of carbon and this element. Carbon bonds to this element so strongly that compounds called PFAS, which contain many such bonds, are nicknamed “forever chemicals.”
tossups.r: That plastic, Teflon, coats nonstick pans. For 10 points, name this most electronegative element, the lightest halogen.

tossups.p: This element has an oxidation number of −1 in all of its compounds, and in its compounds with oxygen, it even forces oxygen into a positive oxidation state. Atoms of this element are the smallest of all the halogens.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this element with atomic number 9, the most reactive halogen.

tossups.p: During the Manhattan Project, uranium was enriched by turning it into a gas of uranium and this element, a method helped by the fact that this element has only one natural isotope. A radioactive isotope of this element with mass number 18 is used in medical PET scans.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this lightest halogen, whose ion is added to toothpaste to fight cavities.

tossups.p: Xenon can bond to two, four, or six atoms of this element, and krypton also forms a compound with it. Neil Bartlett’s 1962 discovery that noble gases can form compounds used a compound of platinum and this element.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this pale yellow gas with atomic number 9, the most electronegative element.

tossups.p: Surprisingly, the bond holding two atoms of this element together is weaker than the bond in a chlorine molecule, because this element’s tiny atoms crowd their lone pairs close enough to repel. Chlorine also beats this element in electron affinity.
tossups.r: Even so, this element tops Linus Pauling’s electronegativity scale. For 10 points, name this lightest halogen, element number 9.

tossups.p: In 1945, Grand Rapids, Michigan, became the first city to add a compound of this element to its drinking water to prevent tooth decay. Dentists sometimes paint a varnish containing this element onto children’s teeth for the same reason.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this element whose −1 ion, fluoride, is found in most toothpastes.

tossups.p: Even though this element is extremely reactive, its compound with hydrogen forms only a weak acid in water. That acid can etch glass, so it must be stored in plastic bottles, and it is used to etch frosted designs onto glassware.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this element with atomic number 9, the lightest member of the halogens.

tossups.p: Aluminum is made by dissolving its oxide in molten cryolite, a mineral of sodium, aluminum, and this element that was once mined in Greenland. A heavy, nonflammable gas made of sulfur and this element insulates high-voltage electrical equipment.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this pale yellow halogen with atomic number 9, the most electronegative element.

tossups.p: Thomas Midgley Jr. helped develop refrigerant gases containing carbon, chlorine, and this element, which were later found to damage the ozone layer. The 1987 Montreal Protocol phased out those gases, called CFCs.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this element with atomic number 9, which sits just above chlorine in group 17.

tossups.p: Hydrogen gas explodes on contact with this element even in the dark and at very low temperatures, unlike a mixture of hydrogen and chlorine, which needs light to set it off. This element forms compounds with nearly every other element.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this most reactive element, a pale yellow halogen with atomic number 9.

tossups.p: This element’s ion can take the place of hydroxide ions in hydroxyapatite, the mineral that makes up tooth enamel. That swap makes enamel harder for the acids made by mouth bacteria to dissolve, which helps prevent cavities.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this element, whose −1 ion, fluoride, is added to most toothpastes.

tossups.p: This element holds its electrons so tightly that it has the highest first ionization energy of any halogen. Its atoms have the electron configuration 1s² 2s² 2p⁵, one electron short of the next element, neon.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this element with atomic number 9, which forms diatomic molecules of a pale yellow gas.

tossups.p: This element’s name comes from the Latin word for “flow,” because a mineral containing it was added to metal ores to help them melt and flow. That mineral, a compound of calcium and this element, comes in many colors, including purple and green.
tossups.r: The word “fluorescence” also comes from that mineral’s name. For 10 points, name this element with atomic number 9.

clues.t: Element with atomic number 9, the lightest halogen, at the top of group 17
The most electronegative element, with a value of nearly 4 on Pauling’s scale
The most reactive element; it forms compounds with nearly every other element
Its −1 ion, fluoride, is added to toothpaste and drinking water to prevent cavities
A pale yellow gas made of diatomic molecules
Teflon, the nonstick coating on pans, is a plastic made of carbon and this element
Its compound with hydrogen dissolves in water to make a weak acid that etches glass
Named for the mineral fluorite, from the Latin for “flow”; fluorite, made of calcium and this element, is 4 on the Mohs scale
CFCs, refrigerant gases that harmed the ozone layer, contain carbon, chlorine, and this element
Has an oxidation number of −1 in all of its compounds
Seven valence electrons (1s² 2s² 2p⁵), one short of neon; the smallest halogen atom
Henri Moissan isolated it in 1886 by electrolysis, after earlier attempts injured several chemists; he won the 1906 Nobel Prize
In 1945, Grand Rapids, Michigan, became the first city to add its ion to drinking water
André-Marie Ampère suggested its name in an 1812 letter to Humphry Davy
Roy Plunkett discovered Teflon by accident at DuPont in 1938
Carbon bonds to it so strongly that PFAS, full of such bonds, are nicknamed “forever chemicals”
In its compounds with oxygen, it forces oxygen into a positive oxidation state
Has only one stable isotope, mass number 19, which made it useful for enriching uranium in the Manhattan Project
Its radioactive isotope with mass number 18 is used in medical PET scans
Xenon bonds to two, four, or six of its atoms; Neil Bartlett’s 1962 noble gas compound used a platinum compound of it
The bond between two of its atoms is weaker than the bond in a chlorine molecule, and chlorine has a higher electron affinity
Hydrogen explodes with it even in the dark and at very low temperatures
Cryolite, a mineral of sodium, aluminum, and this element once mined in Greenland, is used to make aluminum
A heavy, nonflammable compound of sulfur and this element insulates high-voltage electrical equipment
Its ion replaces hydroxide in hydroxyapatite, making tooth enamel harder to dissolve
George Stokes named “fluorescence” after fluorite, a mineral that can glow under ultraviolet light
Has the highest first ionization energy of any halogen

trap.title: Element, not fluoride
trap.body: Many clues are really about fluoride, this element’s −1 ion, in toothpaste and tap water, so players blurt “fluoride” or the mineral “fluorite.” Those are different answers: the tossup wants the element itself. Chlorine is the other trap, since the two halogens share clues about reactivity, CFCs, and diatomic gases.
trap.fix: If it asks for “this element,” name the element, not its ion or its mineral. Atomic number 9, pale yellow, most electronegative, Moissan, and Teflon point here; chlorine is element 17, a yellow-green gas used to disinfect swimming pools.
trap.line: Real answer line: Fluorine (accept F; do not accept “fluoride”)
